newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Hashimoto seek to avoid trade surplus rise.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Hashimoto seek to avoid trade surplus rise.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday said they agreed that Japan should avoid a big rise in its trade surplus with the United States and concentrate on boosting its domestic economies.

The discussion on trade and U.S. worries that hard-won gains in reducing its huge trade deficit with Japan will be reversed by Japan's sluggish economy and weak yen were part of three hours of talks between the two leaders on Friday.
"We both want to promote strong domestic demand-led growth in Japan, and to avoid a significant increase in Japan's external surplus," Clinton said at a news conference with Hashimoto.

U.S. manufacturers, especially the Big Three car makers, have complained that they are being hurt by the weak yen, which makes Japanese goods cheaper in global markets, and the strong dollar, which makes U.S. goods more expensive.

The U.S. trade deficit with Japan fell by 19 percent last year to nearly $48 billion, its lowest level since 1991. But some officials fear those gains will be quickly reversed due to surging imports from Japan, particularly car imports.
Japan's surplus with the United States has been rising over the past six months from year-earlier levels. It rose to $3.04 billion in March, up 11.2 percent from March 1996.
Clinton said he does not believe currency exchange markets should be used to gain undue advantage in global trade.
"We do not want a weak dollar simply to improve our trade position," he said. "That is not our economic policy, to go out and seek a weak dollar." Clinton said.
He added the United States wants a strong, healthy dollar, which reflects its strong economy.
"But neither do we want any other actions to have the effect of throwing the exchange rate system out of whack in order to gain undue advantage in international trade," Clinton said.
Hashimoto said he and Clinton touched on currencies in their discussions and that they would leave further talks on the matter to their finance ministers.
The finance ministers of the Group of Seven major industrial nations are scheduled to meet on Sunday to talk about exchange rates and other economic issues.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters on Friday that he was concerned about the weak yen, but that U.S. dollar policy remains unchanged.
The G7 comprises Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
He noted that the United States "clearly" has had a strong dollar. But at the same time, the economy has been growing strongly for some time.

Rubin responded to criticisms by U.S. car makers and other manufacturers about his strong dollar policy by saying that the U.S. focus should be on improving its own competitiveness, not through attempted manipulation of exchange rates.
The United States is looking for Japan to do more to boost its domestic demand and to deregulate its economy to free its markets up to more foreign products.

Clinton and Hashimoto said they agreed to intensify talks on Tokyo's deregulation efforts. U.S. officials want to ensure that Japan's deregulation efforts will indeed help open its markets to more foreign-made goods.
